'''''Dryopteris erythrosora''''', the '''autumn fern''' or '''Japanese shield fern''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[fern]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Dryopteridaceae, [[native plant|native]] to China South-Central, China Southeast, [[Japan]], [[Korea]], [[Ryukyu Islands|Nansei-shoto]] and [[Taiwan]].<ref name=POWO/>

==Etymology==
The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]], ''erythrosora'', is derived from two [[Ancient Greek]] words, {{lang|grc|ἐρυθρός}} ({{grc-transl|ἐρυθρός}}) meaning red, and {{lang|grc|σωρός}} ({{grc-transl|σωρός}}) meaning heap.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://botanicalepithets.net/dictionary/dictionary.83.html|title=Dictionary of Botanical Epithets|access-date=17 July 2023}}</ref> So ''erythrosora'' literally means red heap, referring to the red [[sorus|sori]] on the undersides of the [[Pinnule|pinnules]]. The specific epithet may really be a reference to the red [[Sorus#Structure|indusia]], which cover the sori.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Horrocks|first=James R.|date=Fall 2003|title=''D. erythrosora''|url=https://hardyferns.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Fall-2003.pdf#page=10|magazine=Hardy Fern Foundation Quarterly|location=Medina, WA|publisher=Hardy Fern Foundation|volume=13|issue=4|page=104|issn=1542-5517|quote=The species name literally means “red sori”, actually referring to the bright red indusia which covers the young sori.|access-date=17 July 2023}}</ref>

The [[common name]], "autumn fern", refers to the coppery-red colour of the emerging fronds, which, even in spring, gives the fern an [[Autumn leaf colour|autumnal appearance]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Rice|first1=Graham|location=[[London]]|title=Get growing: hardy ferns|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/articles/graham-rice/perennials-and-bulbs/starter-ferns|website=[[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS]]|language=en-gb|publisher=[[The Royal Horticultural Society]]|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241016070945/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/articles/graham-rice/perennials-and-bulbs/starter-ferns|archive-date=2024-10-16|access-date=2025-03-24|quote=The common name for ''Dryopteris erythrosora'' is the autumn fern – perversely, because although the evergreen fronds are the colour of autumn foliage they develop their pink or red colouring as they emerge in spring then mature to dark glossy green.}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Autumn Brilliance Fern close-up.jpg|thumb|left|''D. erythrosora'' 'Brilliance']]
It is [[semi-evergreen]] (in cooler climates), with bipinnate [[frond]]s {{convert|30|-|70|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall by {{convert|15|-|35|cm|0|abbr=on}} broad, with 8–20 pairs of pinnae. The fronds have a coppery tint when young, but mature to dark green. It has an upright to down-lying [[rhizome]] which is thick and branched, so that it forms several crowns.

The leaves are funnel-shaped with the top ones being leathery shiny, divided twice, triangular in shape and pointy. The individual leaflets are narrow [[lanceolate]]. Its edge is almost completely sown up.

The [[leaf stalk]]s are about a third as long as the leaf, striated, yellow to red, with linear to lancet-shaped brown scales, containing two large and several small vascular bundles in a cross-sectional drawing.

When budding, the young fronds are coppery red and later green. There can also be several leaf outlets per year. The [[spore]]s, which are kidney-shaped, become ripe between summer and autumn.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Dryopteris erythrosora'' can tolerate a drier soil than many ferns, but is most successful in moist, humus-rich soil, with a pH range of 6.1 to 7.5, with morning or late afternoon sunshine but not during the middle of the day.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Dryopteris erythrosora (Autumn Fern, Japanese Shield Fern, Shaggy Shield Fern) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/dryopteris-erythrosora/|access-date=2021-02-22|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> It is [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] [[hardiness zone|zones]] 5 to 11. Propagation is by division in spring, separating the small crowns from the larger crowns, or by spores. It is raised as an [[ornamental plant]] in gardens because of its color change in the foliage, which change from dark red to dark green, but not very often.<ref>Edward F. Gilman: Dryopteris erythrosis . Fact Sheet FPS-189, Environmental Horticulture Department, Florida Cooperative Extension Service, Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, University of Florida, 1999.</ref>

''D. erythrosora''<ref>{{cite web|title=''D. erythrosora''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/25899/Dryopteris-erythrosora/Details|date=2023|website=RHS|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=17 July 2023}}</ref> and the [[cultivar]] ''D. erythrosora'' 'Brilliance'<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/219161/dryopteris-erythrosora-brilliance/details|title=''D. erythrosora'' 'Brilliance'|date=2023|website=RHS|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=17 July 2023}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf#page=40|title=AGM Plants – Ornamental|date=April 2023|page=40|website=RHS|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=17 July 2023}}</ref>
